results.why: Deck B has a deeper, more coherent control suite. It runs 4 No More Lies, Three Steps Ahead, 4 Lightning Helix and 3 Get Lost, which answers far more threats than Deck A's thin mix of Sear, Firebending Lesson and only 3 counterspells. Deck A also spends slots on marginal cards like Flashback and a lone North Wind Avatar, and its mana casts spells less reliably early (85% vs 94.5% on turn 1).

Deck A runs the established Lute control shell: Resonating Lute ramps into Jeskai Revelation and big Traumatic Critiques. Its interaction suite is denser and higher quality, with 4 Helix, 4 No More Lies, 3 Get Lost and Three Steps Ahead, and its mana casts spells more reliably in the early turns. Deck B is weaker on both counts: Flashback, Firebending Lesson and a lone North Wind Avatar are clunkier, it has fewer counters, and Tablet of Discovery is a weaker engine than Lute.

Deck B is a coherent green ramp deck: 12 one- and two-mana dorks, Formidable Speaker and Nature's Rhythm as tutors, and Craterhoof, Ouroboroid and Jolly Balloon Man as payoffs. Its 20 lands look light on paper (25% screw in the goldfish), but the dorks make up for it, and it has real red sources for Balloon Man. Deck A is an unfocused Bant pile of Stormchaser's Talent, Boomerang Basics and a splashed Balloon Man with almost no red mana and no clear win condition.

Deck A has a coherent Golgari-style ramp shell: 16 mana creatures, Nature's Rhythm and Formidable Speaker as tutors, and Ouroboroid, Craterhoof and Balloon Man copies as payoffs. Its mulligan rate is low and its castability is solid. Deck B is 61 cards with no real win condition, a lone Jolly Balloon Man with almost no red mana, and Stormchaser's Talent with few spells to support it. It also mulligans far more often.

Deck A runs the stronger equipment core: four Leyline Axe, cheap-equip Boots and Dragonfire Blade, all made cheaper by Mauler, Kíli and Dwalin. Four Thorin, Mountain-king add a removal-plus-finisher, and four Lonely Mountains are well supported by 15 Equipment. Its mana numbers are also better, while Deck B dilutes the synergy with Spider-Suit and a lone Mjölnir and runs a shakier basic split, though its burn does give it more interaction.

Deck A is a clean 60 with a coherent Dwarf-equipment core and seven cheap burn spells, so it can clear blockers and answer opposing threats. Deck B is 62 cards with no real interaction beyond Thorin's fight trigger. It also runs Doc Ock's Tentacles with no five-drops to trigger it, and Raubahn is a non-Dwarf that can't use Cavern of Souls. Both mana bases are fine, so Deck A's tighter build and removal make it the better tournament pick.

Deck B is a tight mono-black aristocrats shell with flawless mana and strong internal synergy. Popular Egotist and Sackville triggers target the opponent, which are crimes that rebuy Forsaken Miner, and Bloodghast, Nine-Lives Familiar and Rat King give recursive sacrifice fodder. Deck A splashes red for Biotech Specialist on a thin, awkward base, runs only 21 lands with a 22% screw rate, and its plan is less focused despite Rottenmouth Viper's power.

Deck A is a clean mono-black aristocrats list. Recursive bodies (Bloodghast, Forsaken Miner triggered by its own removal, Nine-Lives Familiar) feed Popular Egotist, Sackville-Bagginses and Zealot, and its mana is near-flawless, with 99%+ castability and little screw. Deck B splashes red for four Biotech Specialists across a shaky 21-land manabase, giving 22% screw and only 85% turn-1 castability, so the upside of Rottenmouth Viper doesn't make up for the inconsistency.

Deck B is tighter and more coherent. It pairs cheap, efficient interaction (Burst Lightning, Get Lost, Sear, Helix, 4 Solitary Cell) with a full set of the 3-mana Ajani and Voice of Victory, which protects its planeswalkers on its own turn, all on cleaner two-color mana. Deck A is spread across one-ofs (Mind Stone, Iceberg, Spark Hunter) and runs colorless or utility lands (Fountainport, Sunken Citadel) that strain its WW and RR costs, and its Day of Judgment clashes with its own token plan.

Deck A is a tight Boros superfriends list. It packs fifteen cheap interaction spells, and Voice of Victory protects early and shuts off counterspells during your turn. Its 24 lands are all colored, which shows in the better turn 2-4 castability numbers. Deck B has real synergy (Caretaker's Talent with token walkers, Day of Judgment), but it runs scattered one-ofs, three colorless Fountainports and a tapped Sunken Citadel against RR/WW costs, and generally weaker card quality.

Deck A is the coherent Nykthos/Badgermole Cub ramp shell: 4 Nykthos, Spider Manifestation for green devotion and untaps, and Nature's Rhythm plus Invasion of Ikoria as tutors into a sharp toolbox of Craterhoof, Emrakul, Bahamut and Titan. Deck B dilutes the ramp plan with fair midrange pieces like Kiora, Outcaster Trailblazer and Life's Legacy, and runs only 2 Nykthos. B's 20 lands also leave it screwed about 25% of the time by turn 4, which is worse than A's higher mulligan rate.

Deck A pairs its fast mana with real payoffs and card flow: Ouroboroid, Kiora, and Outcaster Trailblazer all reward the Cub and Trudge ramp, and Fight Rigging has Craterhoof, Ghalta, and Ouroboroid-grown creatures to flip. Deck B points seven tutors at a thin, clunky top end. Emrakul is weak in a mono-green graveyard, Bahamut is a 9-mana saga, and it gives up the engines for clumsier Invasion and Spider Manifestation slots. B's mana is somewhat steadier, but A's plan is more coherent and powerful.

Deck A is a recognizable Boros Heroic build: Monstrous Rage, Swiftspear and Ancestral Anger give it far more damage per card than B's slower counter spells. Its mana also simulates better, with less screw and more consistent land drops. Deck B's mono-white plan is coherent but lower-powered, with a lot of do-nothing pump and protection.

Deck B is much closer to the proven Boros Heroic shell. Swiftspear, Monstrous Rage, Ancestral Anger and Reckless Rage add the cheap red pump and removal that make Hoplite and Virtuoso threatening, and its mana sim shows less screw and better castability. Its 20 lands and Speedball are a bit loose, but Deck A's mono-white build is slower and weaker. Phalanx Leader, Hero of Iroas and non-heroic Hallowblade lean on clunky 2-3 mana sorceries, and its sim shows worse screw numbers.

Deck B has a more complete control suite: No More Lies covers stack threats, Sear and Get Lost handle creatures, planeswalkers and enchantments, and Supreme Verdict plus The Wandering Emperor are proven finishers. Deck A leans on narrow cards like Fiery Impulse, Flashback and the clunky Together as One and has no counterspells. The two decks' mana is roughly comparable, so B's stronger card quality decides it.

Deck A has a fuller control shell: No More Lies, Supreme Verdict, Sear, Get Lost and The Wandering Emperor protect the Revelation/Defeat top end and answer opposing threats on the stack. Deck B has no counterspells, leans on narrow burn like Fiery Impulse, and runs a clunky Together as One. B's mana sims slightly better, but A's mana is still fine at 26 lands with good fixing, so the stronger card suite wins out.

Deck A is a clean two-colour Simic shell. Up the Beanstalk draws off Crab and Terror because they keep mana value 7, Town and Boomerang Basics rebuy Talent and Beanstalk, and its cheap spells fill the graveyard. Its mana casts its hand 89-98% of the time from turn 1. Deck B stretches into a third colour just for Bushwhack, which leaves it able to cast its hand only about 50% of the time on turn 1, even with lots of removal.

Deck A is a coherent Temur Terror/Crab tempo list. It has a dense suite of cheap instants and sorceries that both fuel the delve-style threats and actually interact: Fiery Impulse, Burst Lightning, Axe, Critique, Pierce and Charm. Deck B has cute Up the Beanstalk synergy with the 7-drops, but its only answers are bounce and Bushwhack fights, so it has no real removal, and its mana sims show worse screw and land-drop numbers despite being two colors.

Deck B runs four Faithless Looting, which is banned in Modern, so it is not tournament-legal as built. Deck A is a legal, coherent mono-black Archon reanimator package. It has self-mill (Supplier, Overlord, Emperor), Persist and Flare to cheat Archons, and clean mana that casts everything on curve.

Deck B is a cohesive mono-black Archon reanimator shell. Overlord, Emperor of Bones, Phyrexian Tower, Crypt of Agadeem, and Troll/Street Wraith cycling all feed the Persist/Archon plan, and the one-color mana casts its spells perfectly in the sim with less screw. Deck A has a weaker two-color manabase and filler like Detective's Phoenix, Den of the Bugbear, and redundant sac-draw spells, which dilute the plan.

Deck A is the coherent Eldrazi Ramp shell: Green Sun's Zenith finds Fanatic of Rhonas, Slumbering Trudge or Dryad Arbor, and Fanatic's ferocious mana pairs with Trudge and Fight Rigging to cheat or hard-cast Emrakul and Ulamog. Its MDFC lands also give it real land density despite the slightly worse goldfish numbers. Deck B's Utopia Sprawl, Halfling and Talisman package clashes with its Temple and Labyrinth colorless base, has only 9 Forests for Sprawl, and runs a thinner, weaker top end.

Deck B is the tuned Eldrazi ramp shell. Fanatic of Rhonas pairs with Slumbering Trudge for explosive mana, Green Sun's Zenith fetches Fanatic, Dryad Arbor or Disciple, and Ugin, Eye of the Storms plus Ulamog give it top-end threats that also interact. Deck A gets slightly smoother goldfish mana, but it relies on weaker pieces like Utopia Sprawl with only 9 Forests, off-color Talismans and clunky Turntimber Symbiosis, and its payoffs are thinner, so B is the stronger tournament choice.

Deck B is a coherent UB storm shell. Dark Ritual, LED, Infernal Tutor, Brainstorm and Paradoxical Outcome all feed a Tendrils kill, and 12 real lands including duals and fetches give reliable blue and black. Deck A runs only about 10 lands with just two Volcanic Islands plus the MDFCs for colored mana, includes Ovalchase Daredevil with no black land, and relies on clunky Class enchantments and a lone Gamble-Grapeshot finish, so its mana and plan are much shakier.

Deck A is a coherent UB artifact-storm shell: Rituals, Brainstorm, Infernal Tutor/LED and Paradoxical Outcome, with Tendrils as the finisher. Its 13 lands plus fetches reliably produce U and B, and its goldfish numbers are clearly better. Deck B runs only 10 real lands, 8 of them colorless (Tomb/Saga), with just 2 Volcanic Islands for a deck full of U-costed cards like Echo (UU), Riddlesmith and Does Machines, so it mulligans and stumbles far more often.

Deck B is a coherent Legacy Phoenix list. Faithless Looting and Buried Alive bin Phoenixes, and free or cheap spells like Mutagenic Growth, Gut Shot, Lava Dart with flashback, Ritual and Brainstorm reliably hit three instants or sorceries a turn, all on a solid 16-land Grixis base. Deck A dilutes the plan with four copies of a legendary three-mana vehicle and lacks free spells to rebuy Phoenix, and its slightly better goldfish numbers don't make up for the weaker game plan.

Deck A is the purer Phoenix shell: Faithless Looting and Buried Alive bin the birds, and free or cheap spells like Mutagenic Growth, Gut Shot, Lava Dart and Dark Ritual reliably reach the three instants and sorceries needed to return them. It also has reach with Bolt. Deck B spends slots on clunky Fantasticars and has fewer cheap ways to chain spells, so its plan is less consistent despite slightly smoother goldfish castability numbers.

Deck B is a coherent Boros artifact shell: Glint Hawk and Kor Skyfisher rebuy artifact lands, Galvanic Blast gets metalcraft, and Bolt, Journey and Thraben Charm give it real interaction. Its 18 lands with dual artifact lands make a sound manabase. Deck A runs only 14 lands (52% screw by turn 4), has zero interaction, and spends slots on filler like Phyrexian Walker in a go-wide pile that folds to sweepers and removal.

Deck A is a coherent Boros artifact aggro shell. It pairs a metalcraft creature base and the Glint Hawk/Kor Skyfisher engine with real interaction: Bolt, Galvanic Blast, Journey and Thraben Charm. Deck B is a mono-white go-wide pile running only 14 lands and zero removal, and its sim shows far more mulligans and screw, with no way to answer opposing threats.

Deck B is a coherent Boros aggro list with real removal (Bolt, Journey, Lava Dart), efficient two-drops and a sensible Eidolon/Mascot/Thrilling Discovery value package. Deck A mashes together a Tireless Tribe/Inside Out combo with only one Fling, discard-only Sneaky Snackers and slow Eidolons, so none of its plans is reliable. Its castability numbers also trail Deck B's badly from turn 2 on.

Deck A is a coherent Boros aggro-midrange list with 18 lands that all make its colors, and its castability numbers are strong. It has real removal in Bolt and Journey, efficient threats, and Eidolons that recur off its many gold cards. Deck B's Tireless Tribe/Inside Out combo is fragile, and running four uncastable Sneaky Snackers as discard fodder drags its castability below 50% by turn 4, so it is far less consistent.

Deck B is a coherent Survival/Rector build. Survival of the Fittest, Karmic Guide, Squee, Deranged Hermit and Goblin Bombardment give it a real engine and kill, and Rector can fetch Pattern of Rebirth, Bombardment or Future Sight. Deck A is an unfocused pile with no clear win condition: Decree of Silence and Gaea's Blessing don't close games, and it has few sacrifice outlets to make Rector and Veteran Explorer work, while its mana is no better than B's.

Deck A is a coherent Survival/Rector toolbox. Rector and Pattern find Survival, Bombardment or Future Sight, and Survival chains into Karmic Guide, Squee, Hermit and Wurm for real value and kill engines. Deck B has no real win condition: Decree of Silence only counters three spells, and Gaea's Blessing and Tusker do little, so it's a pile of card draw and removal around a weak Rector target, and its slightly better mana numbers don't make up for that.

Deck B is a coherent, fast reanimator shell. Putrid Imp, Survival, and Buried Alive bin fat targets, then Exhume, Reanimate, and Animate Dead bring them back on turns 1–2, backed by Rituals, Petals, and Therapy, and its low curve makes 16 lands fine (it can cast its hand ~99% of the time). Deck A is a muddled Sneak/Survival pile with uncastable or awkward cards (Nicol Bolas with almost no blue, Phantom Nishoba with almost no white, Genesis, Rhystic Tutor) and diluted payoff density.

Deck B is a recognizable Survival/Sneak Attack shell. Sneak Attack into a hasty double-striking Dragon Tyrant or Colossus is a real kill, and Fiend, Therapy and Duress protect it. Its 22 lands plus 8 mana creatures give much steadier mana, though Phantom Nishoba and Bolas are clunky inclusions. Deck A's reanimator package has few and weak targets (Colossus's sacrifice hurts you after Reanimate's life loss, and Exhume helps the opponent), and it gets screwed far too often on 16 lands.
